notes.bp: Spontaneous speech becomes shorter and less distinct when people speak quickly, so a system or scientist must connect timing to the shape of the vowel space.
notes.wh: Reduction is not one event: speakers can centralize vowels, compress time, or do both, and a global measure may hide that interaction.
notes.naive: Use articulation rate or vowel-space size alone as a complete explanation.
notes.ap: Model spatial vowel distinctiveness and temporal rate together and test whether their interaction predicts non-lexicalized reductions.
notes.mech: French spontaneous speech is measured with pVSA, VDI, articulation rate, and temporally compressed speech zones.
notes.math: Regression separates spatial predictors, temporal predictors, and their interaction rather than treating one acoustic number as the cause.
notes.ww: Smaller vowel space predicts more reduction only when articulation rate is included; rate is the strongest predictor and VDI is not significant.
notes.limits: The French speakers, spontaneous tasks, reduction definition, and acoustic measures bound the result; other languages and conversational settings remain open.
notes.title: Speech Reduction in French: The Relationship Between Vowel Space and Articulation Dynamics

notes.bp: A learner must hear and produce an unfamiliar vowel contrast whose important evidence changes over time rather than staying at one frequency point.
notes.wh: Similar categories overlap, and static formant snapshots miss the movement that distinguishes them.
notes.naive: Measure one midpoint formant and treat perception and production as separate abilities.
notes.ap: Track vowel-inherent spectral change across the vowel and compare perception-production alignment with proficiency and immersion experience.
notes.mech: Polish learners produce and perceive English /e-æ/ and /i-I/; dynamic formant movement is measured over vowel duration.
notes.math: Formant trajectories are time-varying objects; accuracy and production consistency test whether the moving cue is learned.
notes.ww: Advanced learners improve, especially for /i-I/; formant movement increases with proficiency, while length of residence is not significant.
notes.limits: The learner group, contrasts, language experience, and measurements bound the result; other L1s and natural interaction need separate evidence.
notes.title: Influence of Proficiency and L2 Experience on Dynamic Spectral Cue Utilization in L2 Vowel Perception and Production

notes.bp: A streaming system must reconstruct an audio waveform from a magnitude spectrogram without paying a large compute or latency cost.
notes.wh: Magnitude says how much energy is present but not the phase relationships needed to make the waveform line up in time.
notes.naive: Use a large neural inverse model or solve the reconstruction problem with a generic expensive least-squares routine.
notes.ap: Predict phase derivatives with a tiny network and exploit the tridiagonal positive-semidefinite structure of the resulting least-squares system.
notes.mech: The online inversion model uses 8k parameters, adds at most one hop of latency, and applies a linear-complexity solver after predicting derivative information.
notes.math: Phase reconstruction becomes a structured inverse problem; the solver uses matrix structure instead of treating every coefficient as unrelated.
notes.ww: The paper reports a 30x smaller network, a further halving of neural cost with one-hop latency, and orders-of-magnitude solver speedup while retaining quality.
notes.limits: Spectrogram settings, audio domain, latency definition, and samples bound the claim; listening tests and hardware deployment remain separate checks.
notes.title: Efficient Neural and Numerical Methods for High-QualityOnline Speech Spectrogram Inversion via Gradient Theorem

notes.bp: In a multiparty conversation, gestures and pauses should be understood as timed coordination rather than unrelated events.
notes.wh: A pause can occur within one speaker's turn or between speakers, and gesture timing may reflect planning, turn exchange, or social behavior.
notes.naive: Count gestures and pauses independently or align every gesture only to the nearest word.
notes.ap: Measure gesture category, pause type, duration, and onset/offset timing together in annotated audiovisual dialogues.
notes.mech: MULTISIMO recordings provide multiparty dialogue annotations; distributions and temporal relations are compared for within- and between-speaker pauses.
notes.math: The unit of analysis is a timed relation among gesture, pause, and speaker turn; duration and onset timing carry different information.
notes.ww: Self-adaptors align with longer pauses, utterance-final syntax shortens pauses, and most gestured pauses occur within utterances.
notes.limits: Corpus annotation, participant population, gesture categories, and observational design bound the result; causal cognitive interpretations remain hypotheses.
notes.title: Multimodal Dynamics of Hand Gestures and Pauses in Multiparty Interactions

notes.bp: A meeting summarizer should be judged for preserving important facts and staying concise even when no reference summary exists.
notes.wh: Long meetings contain many valid summaries, and reference overlap rewards wording rather than whether the important decisions survived.
notes.naive: Compare generated text with one reference using lexical similarity or ask an LLM for one unstructured score.
notes.ap: Use fact alignment and comparison-based judging, then rank systems with an Elo procedure instead of requiring a reference summary.
notes.mech: CREAM uses reasoning traces and key-fact alignment to compare meeting summaries for completeness and conciseness without references.
notes.math: Fact coverage and brevity become comparison evidence; Elo aggregates pairwise preferences while avoiding a false absolute scale.
notes.ww: The paper presents a reference-free evaluation framework for meeting summarization and reports its ability to rank systems/prompts.
notes.limits: Facts, judge prompts, meeting domain, and pairwise comparison protocol bound the result; human validation and adversarial summaries remain open.
notes.title: Comparison-Based Automatic Evaluation for Meeting Summarization

notes.bp: A speech-quality or emotion model should account for the fact that listeners use different personal rating scales.
notes.wh: Averaging ordinal ratings can invent distances and erase systematic listener differences.
notes.naive: Average all ratings into one target and train a model to reproduce that mean.
notes.ap: Learn a unified listener scale from pairwise comparisons so the ordering of utterances is preserved without assuming numeric distances.
notes.mech: The method is evaluated on speech quality assessment and continuous emotion recognition, comparing a unified comparison-based scale with mean-listener and multi-scale approaches.
notes.math: Pairwise comparison models order utterances; the central mathematical choice is to preserve ordinal relationships rather than average incompatible numbers.
notes.ww: The paper reports improved prediction performance and robustness on both tasks.
notes.limits: Listener panels, rating prompts, comparison construction, and datasets bound the result; agreement and usefulness for new listener populations remain open.
notes.title: Unifying Listener Scoring Scales: Comparison Learning Framework for Speech Quality Assessment and Continuous Speech Emotion Recognition

notes.bp: A system should predict how hard it is to listen to speech in noise, not merely whether the speech is technically intelligible.
notes.wh: Listeners can reconstruct words by effort even when masking leaves only intermittent speech glimpses, and speaking style changes those glimpses.
notes.naive: Use one global SNR or intelligibility score as a proxy for effort.
notes.ap: Measure high-energy speech glimpses and add speaking-style cues such as pitch range and articulation rate to predict listener effort.
notes.mech: HEGP is computed for habitual and clear-Lombard speech in noise; listening-effort ratings are modeled with spectral balance, F0, and rate measures.
notes.math: The target is subjective effort, while HEGP is a release-from-masking proxy; regression tests whether style explains residual variance.
notes.ww: HEGP predicts effort similarly across styles; wider F0 range and slower articulation are associated with lower effort, especially for habitual speech.
notes.limits: Noise, listener ratings, speech styles, and HEGP definition bound the result; individual strategy and real device conditions remain open.
notes.title: Prediction of listening effort ratings for habitual and clear-Lombard speech presented in noise

notes.bp: Contextual ASR should recognize a large list of names or domain words without being distracted by irrelevant entries.
notes.wh: A large bias list creates search competition and homophone errors, so adding every candidate can hurt the very words it is meant to help.
notes.naive: Pass the full list to decoding or choose entries by frequency alone.
notes.ap: Train a scorer that ranks and selects bias words from an NER-derived list before contextual Whisper decoding.
notes.mech: A bias-word ranking network selects candidates from the IS21 list and evaluates contextual Whisper on LibriSpeech.
notes.math: Selection turns a huge candidate set into a focused conditional recognition problem; biased WER measures the targeted words while overall WER checks collateral damage.
notes.ww: The paper reports more than 40% relative reduction in biased WER from ranking and selection.
notes.limits: NER list, LibriSpeech, Whisper context mechanism, and bias-word definition bound the result; new domains and errors in entity extraction remain open.
notes.title: Ranking and Selection of Bias Words for Contextual Bias Speech Recognition
